title: Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion and Balance Sheet

epigraph.quote: Revenue is vanity, profit is sanity, cash is reality.
epigraph.author: Common business maxim

web_blocks.text: The financial record has two chapters. From FY15 through FY22, the blind snapshot shows revenue between ₹553 crore and ₹1,158 crore, with operating margins mostly in the 6–11% range and small or inconsistent net profits. FY23–FY24 were stronger but still modest. FY25 and FY26 brought a step-change: consolidated sales rose to ₹2,019 crore and ₹2,509 crore, operating EBITDA to ₹327 crore and ₹383 crore, and PAT to ₹216 crore and ₹272 crore. This is genuine earnings growth, but it is concentrated in a short recent window and coincides with an industry upcycle and capacity expansion. [1][17][26]

web_blocks.takeaway: The five-year picture is not a straight-line compounding record: FY25 cash conversion was strong, while FY26 reversed sharply. [1][17]

web_blocks.text: A closer look at FY26 reported income separates repeatable operating progress from less repeatable items. Consolidated operating EBITDA was ₹383 crore, while other income was ₹61 crore. The separate EBIT figure was about ₹353 crore after ₹29.91 crore depreciation. The annual report lists interest income, foreign-exchange gains, investment revaluation gains and a ₹24.66 crore provision reversal among other-income components. Those items are not necessarily improper; they simply should not be capitalized as if they were recurring factory margin. The operating story remains strong, but the quality of PAT should be assessed alongside core EBITDA, cash from operations and the working-capital bridge. [1][17]

Debt and liquidity need a facility-by-facility view during expansion. The annual report reports working-capital borrowing growth as an important financing source in FY26, while the cash-flow statement shows ₹187.91 crore of net increase in working-capital borrowings and CFO of negative ₹105.38 crore. This does not by itself imply solvency stress: the company also has a strengthened equity base from the earlier QIP and a profitable operating record. It does mean that interest expense and bank limits can rise if receivables and inventory remain elevated. We cannot calculate a stable net-debt picture from one short-period snapshot without reconciling cash, liquid investments, borrowings, leases and contingent obligations. [1][17][18]

Capital returns are also in transition. The latest FY26 ROCE in company reporting is about 23%, down from approximately 28% in FY25; the blind multi-year snapshot shows earlier returns far lower. The company is adding fixed assets and construction in progress ahead of full utilization, so near-term ROCE may fall before new capacity contributes. The right test is incremental return on the new capital: additional operating EBITDA and cash after tax relative to the cumulative assets and working capital committed. Filings do not disclose a project-level return target, so no precise incremental ROIC estimate is supportable today. [1][17]

Profit growth in FY26 was supported by real operations: consolidated revenue grew 24.2%, EBITDA 17%-ish, and PAT 25.6%; record production reached 33,763 MVA. But the composition matters. Consolidated other income was ₹60.85 crore, including interest income, foreign exchange and provisions written back, while operating cash flow turned negative. The earnings are not fictitious; they are simply not yet matched by cash. [1][17]

Cash conversion is the central forensic issue. CFO fell from ₹156.58 crore in FY25 to negative ₹105.38 crore in FY26, while PAT increased from ₹216.43 crore to ₹272.17 crore. Receivable days rose by 44, inventory days by 15, and payable days fell by 47; the working-capital cycle expanded by more than 100 days. [1][17][27]

The balance sheet has also absorbed growth and capital actions. A ₹500 crore QIP in 2024 added equity financing; fixed assets and capital work in progress rose as capacity expansion proceeded, and reserves increased with retained earnings. The FY26 audited report describes ₹1,000 crore-plus planned investment over the following 15 months, while October 2026 announced new greenfield projects. These investments may improve production control, but returns depend on timing, utilization and cash discipline. [1][5][16]

Return ratios have improved materially from low levels, with the blind snapshot showing ROCE around 23% in FY26 versus 28% in FY25 and much lower levels earlier. The FY26 annual report attributes strong return ratios to improved profitability, while the fall in ROCE reflects capital employed rising ahead of full utilization. Since WACC is not provided by filings and would depend on current market inputs, this chapter does not claim a precise ROIC–WACC spread. The investment case needs returns after the new asset base is deployed, not a peak-year return on the old base. [1][28]

Dilution and per-share comparability require care. The QIP added roughly 7.52 million shares; the 1:1 bonus issue doubled the number of shares. The snapshot’s equity capital increased from ₹13–14 crore historically to ₹30 crore in FY25. EPS comparisons across this transition must be adjusted, and reported profit growth should not be confused with equal growth in per-share intrinsic value. [5][7]

book_paragraphs: Follow the decade and you see a business that was once modest and uneven, then abruptly grew into a much larger earnings machine. Revenue went from roughly ₹700 crore in FY20 to more than ₹2,500 crore in FY26. Operating margins moved from single digits into the mid-teens. That kind of acceleration deserves attention, but the pattern is not yet a decade of stable compounding. It is two powerful years layered on a cyclical manufacturing business.

Now set profit beside cash. FY25 converted a meaningful portion of earnings into operating cash. FY26 did not: the group reported ₹272 crore of PAT but used ₹105 crore of operating cash. Receivables took longer to collect, inventory rose and suppliers were paid sooner. If the company is investing in future growth, this may be a temporary timing burden. If the pattern persists, it becomes a financing requirement that can dilute shareholders or raise debt costs.

The balance sheet is funding both opportunity and friction. Equity raised in 2024 helped pay for a capacity buildout. Capital work in progress and fixed assets increased, and borrowings also rose as working capital expanded. The company plans substantial new capex and integration. You and I should judge each project by commissioning, customer approvals, utilization and cash contribution, not by the number of MVA announced.

Profit quality has encouraging and cautionary elements. The core business generated substantial operating EBITDA and PAT. Other income and provision write-backs also contributed to reported profit, while bad-debt provisions remain a reminder that receivables are not automatically cash. Return on capital remains healthy by the latest reported figures, but has eased from the prior year as investment gets ahead of earnings. A high return on a smaller asset base is not the same as a high return after expansion.

The conclusion is conditional, not because the evidence is vague, but because two observable facts point in different directions. The operating franchise has gained scale and improved margins. Cash conversion has weakened sharply at exactly the moment management is committing more capital. The next financial reports can resolve this tension: if CFO recovers, working capital normalizes and incremental plants earn attractive returns, quality improves. If receivables, inventory and debt keep climbing faster than sales, the earnings curve will overstate the value created.

FY26’s “other income” deserves a quiet but careful read. Interest received and investment-related gains can be useful, and reversing an old provision can be justified when the underlying obligation changes. But these are different from selling more transformers at a better margin. You and I should not strip them away mechanically; instead, we should identify them, compare the operating EBITDA trend, and then ask whether cash followed. Here, operating EBITDA rose substantially, but operating cash flow turned negative. That is why the gap matters more than any single adjustment.

The funding mechanism is visible in the audited cash-flow statement. The company generated ₹409.63 crore of cash from operations before working-capital changes. Receivables and inventories absorbed cash, and supplier payments reduced the financing cushion. The company increased working-capital borrowings by ₹187.91 crore. This is a coherent explanation for the negative cash-flow year, but explanations do not end the test. Collections must arrive, work-in-progress must convert into accepted equipment, and the borrowing increase must reverse or at least grow more slowly than earnings.

Now consider the capital being installed. A new production line can add volume without adding the same amount of labor per unit, which is the route to operating leverage. But the initial years carry construction cash outflow, depreciation, qualification work and lower utilization. That sequence can compress return ratios before they improve. We should compare the assets added with the incremental operating EBITDA once the line is fully active, while also accounting for the working capital needed to fill it. Capacity only creates value when the new machine is both utilized and paid for by the customer.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: TARIL has demonstrated operating leverage. It has not yet demonstrated that the expanded business can grow without consuming disproportionate cash.
